note: The path. The corridor is geometry of its own now, so the maps of the paving are the path's own and not the ground's. They DISPLACE terrain-detail and terrain-path, which are declared in V1's fragment with a note saying they are V3's to claim when this happened: nothing here moves them, because that fragment is another session's file, but the corridor reads neither, and the day the ground stops painting a path under this one the first frame gets 731 kB back. THREE ENTRIES AND NOT ONE, and every split is a measurement rather than a filing habit. The ruler and the level of the piece want different pitches and compress in opposite ways: carried in one two-channel texture they cost 1 407 kB and apart they cost 731, because the ruler's pitch is set by the finest joint that has to survive being sampled while the level is piecewise constant on pieces a hand across. The field of small stones is laid over the WORLD and not along the run, so it could not have shared a coordinate with either of them at any price. None of the three is a picture and none may ever go through a block codec: two are rulers and one repeats over the whole run, and what a codec puts into a fine grain repeated over the whole run is its own block pattern, everywhere.

assets.note: how deep inside the nearest slot of the paving a point stands, laid along the run instead of over the world: the corridor is a ribbon a metre across and forty long, so a square texture over the world would spend all but a fortieth of itself on meadow with no joints in it. Nought over all the stone, growing into the joint, clamped at 48 mm - the deepest a point can be inside the widest joint the reference has - which is 0.188 mm to a code. IT IS THE SEED'S OWN DISTANCE FIELD WITH THE DIRECTION REVERSED, and the reversal is a reading and not a convenience. The seed stored how far the nearest joint EDGE was and let the ground atlas say what was INSIDE the joint; this corridor has no atlas, so the one field it stores has to carry the joint's cross section as well as its edge. Across its own width the reference's joint stands 16.7% brighter within a centimetre of stone than more than two from any - the broken lip of two pieces at the sides and soil in the middle - and a field measured INTO the slot gives that for nothing, where a milled slot of one tone answers nought. Every property the seed argued for survives the flip: unsigned, so the mean over a mip footprint moves AWAY from nought and a joint thins with distance instead of a false one appearing in the middle of a slab; and the edge is the crossing of nought, which is a POSITION and interpolates, so the frame draws an edge finer than the texel that told it where the edge was. The pitch is 7.81 mm across the run by 8.40 mm along it, very nearly isotropic because the lattice is turned and its joints therefore run at every bearing; the joints of the reference are 8 mm at the first decile, and a joint narrower than the pitch does not blur, it VANISHES between two samples

the level of the piece of paving under a point, nought for the earth between and over the pieces and one for the palest slab, on the same strip and at a quarter of the ruler's pitch. It is PIECEWISE CONSTANT by construction, and that is the whole of why it is a map at all: a field asked per POINT instead of per PIECE crosses joints, and a stain that crosses a joint welds two slabs into one thing, which is the defect the committente threw out three times. What its pitch has to be finer than is a PIECE and not a joint - at 19.5 by 21.0 mm a piece of 15 cm is eight texels across, and the ramp a bilinear tap draws at a piece boundary is half the width of the median joint drawn over it. Below that the ramp gets wider than the joint and two pieces begin borrowing each other's level, which is the one thing the identity between slabs cannot survive: the reference spreads its level between one piece and the next by 0.0695 against 0.0888 within one, a ratio of 0.78, and a paving that blurred the first would answer that reading upside down. It is not supersampled when it is painted, for the same reason: averaging over a texel's footprint would blur the one boundary this map has any structure at

the small stones of the paving and the grain of the stone, over 1.592 m of ground to a repeat and turned nineteen degrees off the run. RED is the field of the small stones, a half AT the rim and above it inside, so the rim is a crossing and interpolates and a 2.8 cm stone is drawn as round as the frame likes rather than as round as the tile is; GREEN is the grain, mean a half by construction so it adds material to the stone without moving how bright the stone is. IT IS A TILE AND NOT A STRIP, and that is a measurement: the reference's stones are 2.8 cm at the median and 55% of them lie on a slab against a paving that is 59.5% slab, which within the noise of a count of two hundred is the same number - they are scattered over the ground and do not know where the joints are. A 2.8 cm stone written into the strip beside it, which is 8 mm a texel along the run, comes back three texels long and reads as a stroke down the middle of the path, which is the defect the whole corridor was rebuilt to close. A tile has no atlas and therefore no Nyquist of its own, and its mip chain does the right thing at every distance for free; the turn is what costs the repeat its period along the walk, since stepping down the run moves the tile coordinate by different fractions across and along and the pattern only returns when both are whole repeats. The repeat itself is DERIVED from the count rather than chosen - six seats of 14.2 stones a square metre - so the lattice wraps and the tile closes on itself; a repeat picked as a round number of metres would leave a fraction of a cell at the edge and draw a line down two of its own sides, for ever. The side of the tile is 384 texels and that number is written by the first frame and not by the picture: the grain is very nearly incompressible - 302 kB of the 358 the pair cost at 512 against 23 for the field of stones beside it - and 4.15 mm a texel still leaves the finest octave of it 4.6 texels to a cycle
